subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Stellar Mass: A Star's Destiny
description: Learn Stellar Mass: A Star's Destiny in one minute.

hook.text: A star's mass at birth determines everything—its color, brightness, lifespan, and how it will die.

buildup.text: Heavy stars burn hot and blue, dying in millions of years. Light stars glow red and last trillions of years.

discovery.text: Our Sun is mid-range. It will live about 10 billion years—long enough for life to evolve on Earth.

twist.text: The most massive stars are 200 times the Sun's mass. They live only a few million years before exploding.

climax.text: Red dwarfs are the most common stars. They burn so slowly that none born at the Big Bang has died yet.

punchline.text: Born heavy, die fast. Born light, glow forever. Mass is destiny.

quiz.question: Why do massive stars have shorter lifespans than small stars?
options: They burn through their fuel much faster due to higher core temperatures
They lose mass rapidly through powerful solar winds
Their cores collapse under gravity more quickly after forming

details.summary: A star's mass at birth determines virtually everything about its life and death. Low-mass stars burn slowly for trillions of years. Sun-like stars live billions of years and become white dwarfs.
details.whyItMatters: Mass is the single most important property of a star. Knowing a star's mass predicts its color, temperature, luminosity, lifetime, and ultimate fate — making mass the master variable of stellar astrophysics.
takeaways: Mass determines a star's temperature, luminosity, and lifetime
Low-mass stars live trillions of years; massive ones live millions
Final fate — white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole — depends on mass

faq.question: What is the minimum mass for a star?
faq.answer: About 0.08 solar masses — roughly 80 times Jupiter's mass. Below this threshold, core temperatures never reach the 10 million degrees needed for sustained hydrogen fusion. These failed stars are called brown dwarfs, producing some heat but never becoming true stars.

faq.question: What is the maximum mass a star can have?
faq.answer: The theoretical upper limit is around 150-300 solar masses, set by radiation pressure blowing away material during formation. The most massive known stars exceed 100 solar masses. Stars near this limit are extremely rare, luminous, and short-lived.
